title: Does Memory Make You... You?
author: Anya Leonard
summary: The founder of Classical Wisdom uses cognitive-science findings about the unreliability of memory — participants' convinced but inaccurate 9/11 recollections, soldiers' conflicting battle accounts merging via the "co-witness effect" — to build a case for the ancient world's disciplined approach to memory training. She traces memory's role as "a cornerstone of education" from the Pythagoreans' twice-daily review of words and deeds, through the oral bards who recited tens of thousands of lines, to the Method of Loci (the Memory Palace) traditionally attributed to Simonides and used by politicians, rhetoricians and philosophers to commit long speeches to memory without any external aids. Her central move is to reframe the ancients' feats not as products of necessity (no teleprompters, no paper) but as a genuinely cultivated discipline that the modern West has abandoned, treating rote memorization as torture rather than as a trained faculty worth developing. The piece closes on a philosophical question with real stakes for dementia and memory-loss caregivers: if memory is inherently reconstructive and prone to fading without active reinforcement, how much of personal identity actually depends on it.
points: Memory research on major events like 9/11 shows participants hold vivid, high-confidence recollections that are nonetheless demonstrably inconsistent with reality or their own earlier accounts — memory is reconstructive, not a stored recording.

The "co-witness effect" documented among soldiers after battle shows individual memories can merge and conform to each other once people compare notes, complicating the assumption that talking things through simply clarifies what happened.

The Pythagoreans built memory training into daily discipline, reviewing each day's words and deeds every morning and evening and committing their master's teachings to memory before they were ever written down.

The Method of Loci (Memory Palace), traditionally credited to the poet Simonides, works by assigning items to be memorized to specific locations along a familiar mental path — a technique politicians, rhetoricians and philosophers used to commit entire speeches to memory.

The modern West has flipped the ancient valuation of memorization, treating rote learning as "a form of torture" that stifles creativity, even while continuing to admire orators who can recite long passages from memory.
quotes: When researchers, for instance, compared people's memories of major events, such as the September 11 terrorist attacks, they regularly found that participants' recollections, of which they were completely convinced, were often inconsistent with reality...or even with their own earlier accounts.

In many instances, they were only able to make sense of their own individual experiences after discussing the events with their comrades-in-arms, allowing them to place what had happened into a broader context. This, however, could also result in memory conformity, where the memories merge...a phenomenon known as the co-witness effect.

This was something the ancients knew all too well. Memory was a cornerstone of education, enshrined in religion, ritual, as well as everyday life. The Pythagoreans, for example, cultivated memory through daily discipline.
They were expected to review each day's words and deeds every morning and evening, while also committing their master's teachings to memory before they were ever written down.

You then decide upon a specific path through that place before assigning whatever needs memorizing to its different locations. The result is that you simply take your mental walk to remember each item or topic as you go.
We tend to shun rote learning, recalling (ironically) our painful experiences with multiplication tables, and so often view the practice as a form of torture, something that stifles our creativity...
At its most extreme, characters such as Leonard in Christopher Nolan's Memento demonstrate that without the ability to form new memories, life as we know it becomes almost impossible.
